title: Trump Administration orders CDC to change COVID-19 testing guidelines
description_short: Trump Administration orders CDC to change COVID-19 testing guidelines
description_medium: On August 25, 2020, the CDC changed its COVID-19 testing guidance so people without symptoms generally would not be tested, even after a known exposure. The timeline says the White House and Department of Health and Human Services directed the change. It came after Donald Trump had argued that testing should be reduced and while schools were trying to remain open. The entry focuses on a shift in federal public-health advice.
description_long:
On August 25, 2020, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention revised its COVID-19 testing guidance. Under the change described in the timeline, people without symptoms were advised against testing even when they knew they had been exposed to someone with the virus. This moved the guidance away from testing asymptomatic contacts as a routine precaution. The timeline attributes the change to direction from the White House and the Department of Health and Human Services, and places it after Donald Trump had repeatedly argued that fewer tests would make reported case numbers lower.

The timing mattered because schools were attempting to reopen during the pandemic. The source pointed to contemporaneous reports of schools closing after students or staff tested positive, and stressed that people without symptoms could still transmit the virus. The entry therefore records a federal policy change amid active transmission concerns, rather than a new test or a local school rule. It does not quantify how many people were denied tests or establish the change's effects on infections. The documented point is that federal guidance narrowed who was encouraged to test, despite known exposure.

title: Trump: Two dead at Miami Deportation Center since Trump's inauguration
description_short: Trump: Two dead at Miami Deportation Center since Trump's inauguration
description_medium: Maksym Chernyak, a Ukrainian detainee at Miami’s Krome Service Processing Center, died after vomiting and experiencing seizures. Hospital staff found internal bleeding in his brain and pronounced him brain dead. His death on February 24, 2025, was the second reported death at Krome since Donald Trump took office on January 20; another detainee, Genry Donaldo Ruiz-Guillen, died there on January 23. The entry documents two deaths at one immigration detention facility.
description_long:
Maksym Chernyak, a Ukrainian man held at Miami’s Krome Service Processing Center, became ill with vomiting and seizures and was taken to a Miami hospital. Medical staff found internal bleeding in his brain and pronounced him brain dead. His death, reported on February 24, 2025, was the second death of a detainee at Krome since Donald Trump’s inauguration on January 20. The first was Genry Donaldo Ruiz-Guillen, a Honduran man who died on January 23 after detention. ICE said Ruiz-Guillen had experienced dizziness and epileptic seizures for months.

The account situates Chernyak’s death within a facility already facing scrutiny. It describes Krome as an immigration detention center and recounts separate reports about conditions there, including detainees sleeping on floors and restrictions on phone calls. Those conditions are distinct allegations and do not establish the cause of either death. The entry does not provide a medical finding about why Chernyak developed the bleeding or establish whether detention conditions contributed. It records the known sequence, the hospital finding, and the fact that two detainees had died at the same center within weeks, raising questions about detainee health and care that the supplied account does not resolve.

title: E. Jean Carroll Wins $83.3 Million Defamation Judgment Against Trump
description_short: E. Jean Carroll Wins $83.3 Million Defamation Judgment Against Trump
description_medium: On January 26, 2024, a federal jury in New York ordered Donald Trump to pay writer E. Jean Carroll $83.3 million in a defamation case. The award followed a 2023 verdict that found Trump liable for sexual abuse and defamation and awarded Carroll $5 million. The second jury considered Trump’s later denials and attacks on Carroll. Trump rejected the result, said he would appeal, and continued to criticize her publicly.
description_long:
A federal jury in New York ordered Donald Trump to pay E. Jean Carroll $83.3 million on January 26, 2024. The case concerned statements Trump made about Carroll after an earlier jury had found him liable for sexual abuse and defamation. That 2023 verdict resulted in a $5 million award. In the later trial, the jury considered whether Trump’s continued denials and attacks on Carroll’s credibility had defamed her and what damages those statements caused. It returned the much larger award for reputational and personal harm.

The judgment was a civil defamation award, separate from the first case’s $5 million verdict. Judge Lewis Kaplan presided over the proceedings. Trump refused to apologize, said he would appeal, and continued to attack Carroll publicly after the verdict, according to the supplied account. Those responses left the dispute active even after the jury reached its decision. The entry documents the legal consequence of repeated post-verdict statements: a jury found them actionable and set damages at $83.3 million. It does not describe the eventual outcome of any appeal, so the award should be understood here as the jury’s judgment at that point in the case.

title: Trump: Paul Manafort offers updates to Russian oligarch, US-banned Oleg Deripaska
description_short: Trump: Paul Manafort offers updates to Russian oligarch, US-banned Oleg Deripaska
description_medium: In July 2016, Paul Manafort, then Donald Trump’s acting campaign manager, emailed a contact in Russia with a request to pass an offer to Russian oligarch Oleg Deripaska: private campaign briefings could be arranged. The exchange later appeared in emails obtained by Robert Mueller’s investigative team. Representatives for Manafort and Deripaska said the briefings never took place. The record documents an offer, not evidence that the information was delivered.
description_long:
In July 2016, Paul Manafort, serving as Donald Trump’s acting campaign manager, emailed a contact in Russia and asked that a message be passed to Oleg Deripaska. Manafort wrote that private briefings could be arranged if Deripaska wanted them. The exchange later became part of a large collection of Manafort emails obtained by Robert Mueller’s team during its Russia investigation. Deripaska was a Russian business figure who had known ties to Manafort; the timeline also recounts reporting about a failed investment and a claimed debt between them.

The significance of the message is its offer of access to campaign information to a wealthy Russian contact, at a time when Manafort was leading Trump’s campaign. The available account does not show that the proposed briefings actually occurred. Spokespeople for both Manafort and Deripaska said they never materialized. That distinction matters: the record supports the existence of the email and the offer, while the actual transfer of private campaign information remains unestablished in this account. The entry documents the contact and the questions it raised about Manafort’s relationships and campaign role without treating the offer itself as proof that a briefing was held.

title: Trump: Corporations cut ties with Trump and the GOP after insurrection
description_short: Trump: Corporations cut ties with Trump and the GOP after insurrection
description_medium: After the January 6, 2021 attack on the Capitol, companies announced restrictions on political giving to Republicans who had objected to certifying Joe Biden’s election. Dow said it would stop donations to the 147 objecting lawmakers unless they were reelected; Marriott and other companies made similar pledges. Other businesses paused contributions, while Stripe and Shopify separately cut off campaign payment or store services tied to Trump. The entry records several distinct corporate responses.
description_long:
In the days after the January 6, 2021 attack on the Capitol, a number of companies announced changes to their political giving or business relationships involving Donald Trump and Republicans who challenged certification of Joe Biden’s victory. Dow said it would stop donations to the 147 Republican lawmakers who objected, unless they were reelected. Marriott International, Morgan Stanley, and the Blue Cross Blue Shield Association made similar pledges. Coca-Cola, Verizon, AT&T, Comcast, and Facebook were among companies reported to be withholding political contributions temporarily.

Other actions affected Trump’s campaign or businesses more directly. Stripe said it would no longer process payments on the campaign website, Shopify closed several Trump and MAGA online stores, and Deutsche Bank decided not to do future business with Trump or his company after serving as a major lender. Signature Bank also closed two Trump accounts totaling more than $5 million. These were separate decisions with different scopes; a pause in donations was not the same as ending all business ties. Taken together, they show corporate and financial institutions responding to the attack and the congressional objections. The entry does not claim that every company permanently severed every relationship.

title: Trump: NJ official accuses Trump of breaking the law to prevent competition
description_short: Trump: NJ official accuses Trump of breaking the law to prevent competition
description_medium: In April 1997, James Kennedy, head of New Jersey’s Casino Reinvestment Development Authority, asked the state gaming regulator to investigate Donald Trump. Kennedy alleged Trump violated a state law intended to protect casino competition by trying to stop an Atlantic City tunnel that would improve access to a developing casino district. Trump had separately sued to block the project. State officials deferred an investigation while that case was pending; none followed after it was dismissed.
description_long:
On April 22, 1997, James Kennedy, executive director of New Jersey’s Casino Reinvestment Development Authority, asked the state Division of Gaming Enforcement to investigate Donald Trump. Kennedy alleged that Trump had violated a state law designed to preserve competition among casinos by trying to block a tunnel in Atlantic City. The proposed tunnel would make travel easier between the Atlantic City Expressway and the marina district, where hotels and casinos were being developed.

Trump had filed a federal lawsuit in February seeking to stop construction. He argued that Kennedy’s agency was violating the state constitution by funding projects that were not directly intended for elderly or disabled residents, and accused the state of helping his competitors. The New Jersey Attorney General’s office told the gaming authority not to investigate while Trump’s lawsuit remained pending. After the case was dismissed, no investigation of Trump took place. The timeline says Trump spent more than $500,000 fighting the tunnel by the end of July. The episode therefore records an accusation and a blocked regulatory inquiry, not a finding by the state that Trump broke the law.

title: Donald Trump announces 1776 Commission to end black history in schools
description_short: Donald Trump announces 1776 Commission to end black history in schools
description_medium: On September 17, 2020, Donald Trump announced an executive order creating the 1776 Commission, which he presented as a way to promote “patriotic” history in schools. He criticized the New York Times’ 1619 Project and critical race theory, arguing they distorted the nation’s history. The announcement came amid disputes over how schools teach slavery and racism. The entry documents the administration’s attempt to shape that debate through a federal commission.
description_long:
Donald Trump announced an executive order to create the 1776 Commission on September 17, 2020. He described the effort as a way to promote “patriotic” history in schools and argued that Democrats had allowed teaching to place too much emphasis on race and slavery. In the announcement, he attacked the New York Times’ 1619 Project and critical race theory, presenting them as threats to the country. The project and the academic field address the history and continuing effects of slavery and racism, subjects that had become prominent in public debate.

The commission announcement was part of a broader political dispute over curricula, historical interpretation, and how schools discuss the nation’s past. The supplied account characterizes the proposal as pressure on schools to use a more favorable national narrative. It also quotes commentator Ana Kasparian criticizing the implication that students should not learn about racism and slavery. The record documents Trump’s announcement and rhetoric; it does not establish that the commission changed what any particular school taught. The title’s claim that the effort was meant to end Black history is an interpretation of the initiative’s purpose, while the described action itself was the creation of a commission through executive order.

title: Trump: ICE kidnaps & tortures legal immigrant and father at Logan Airport
description_short: Trump: ICE kidnaps & tortures legal immigrant and father at Logan Airport
description_medium: Fabian Schmidt, a New Hampshire resident and green-card holder, was arrested by ICE at Boston’s Logan Airport on March 7, 2025. His family later said agents stripped him, forced him into a cold shower, questioned him while naked, confined him on the floor, and withheld food, water, sleep, and medication. The source says he received medical care after collapsing and was later held in Rhode Island. Physical assault was not established.
description_long:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested Fabian Schmidt at Logan Airport in Massachusetts on March 7, 2025. Schmidt was a New Hampshire resident, a green-card holder, an electrical engineer, a husband, and the father of an eight-year-old girl. His family said that after he disappeared from contact, agents stripped him, forced him into a cold shower, interrogated him while he was naked, and kept him on a mat on the floor. They also alleged that agents denied him food, water, sleep, and his medication. The account says medical care came only after he collapsed.

The allegations are attributed to Schmidt’s family; the source does not independently establish each detail. It states that ICE agents demanded he give up his green card and that Schmidt was being held at the Donald W. Wyatt detention facility in Rhode Island as of March 15. The account says he had lived legally in the United States since 2008 and had no criminal record beyond a decade-old DUI. It is unclear whether he experienced physical assault. The entry documents a detention and serious claims about treatment in custody, while leaving the extent and verification of the alleged conduct unresolved.

description_long:

The timeline names several people involved in the trip and says that in Moscow Trump connected with Felix Sater, a Russian-American businessman whom the source describes as having fled to Russia while facing charges in the United States. It identifies Sater’s father, Mikhail Sheferovsky, as a New York-based underboss for Semion Mogilevich. The source also connects the visit to later business relationships: Trump partnered with Sater’s Bayrock Group on Trump SoHo, and Lorber became an adviser to Trump’s 2016 campaign.
